pumac-2009-geometry-a-07.title: Cut into three triangles
pumac-2009-geometry-a-07.body:
Let $AB=BC=a$, $CD=DE=b$, $AC=p$, $CE=q$ and $\angle BCD=x$ (here $x=165^\circ$; the value of $x$ will turn out not to matter).

By the law of cosines $p^2=2a^2(1-\cos150^\circ)=2a^2(1+\cos30^\circ)$ and $q^2=2b^2(1-\cos30^\circ)$, so $p^2q^2=4a^2b^2(1-\cos^230^\circ)=a^2b^2$ and $pq=ab$.

Triangles $ABC$, $CDE$ are isosceles with base angles $15^\circ$ and $75^\circ$, so $\angle ACE=x-15^\circ-75^\circ=x-90^\circ$. The area is $$[ABC]+[CDE]+[ACE]=\tfrac12a^2\sin150^\circ+\tfrac12b^2\sin30^\circ+\tfrac12pq\sin(x-90^\circ)=\tfrac14\left(a^2+b^2-2ab\cos x\right).$$ By the law of cosines in triangle $BCD$ this is $\frac14BD^2=\frac{36}{4}=9$.

**Answer: 9**

pumac-2009-geometry-a-08.title: Trigonometric Ceva
pumac-2009-geometry-a-08.body:
Let $\beta=\angle MBC$ and $\gamma=\angle MCB$. The angles of the triangle add to $180^\circ$: $(10^\circ+40^\circ)+(20^\circ+\beta)+(30^\circ+\gamma)=180^\circ$, so $\beta+\gamma=80^\circ$.

Trigonometric Ceva for $M$: $$\frac{\sin10^\circ}{\sin40^\circ}\cdot\frac{\sin30^\circ}{\sin\gamma}\cdot\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin20^\circ}=1.$$ Try $\beta=60^\circ$, $\gamma=20^\circ$: the left side is $\frac{\sin10^\circ\cdot\frac12\cdot\sin60^\circ}{\sin40^\circ\sin^220^\circ}$, which equals $1$: it is equivalent to $\sin10^\circ\sin60^\circ=2\sin40^\circ\sin^220^\circ$, and using $\sin20^\circ\sin40^\circ\sin80^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}8$ with $\sin80^\circ=\cos10^\circ$ the right side becomes $\frac{\sqrt3\sin20^\circ}{4\cos10^\circ}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin10^\circ$. Since $\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin(80^\circ-\beta)}$ is increasing in $\beta$ on $(0^\circ,80^\circ)$, the solution is unique, so $\beta=60^\circ$.

**Answer: 60**

pumac-2009-geometry-a-08.title: Show $AM\perp BC$
pumac-2009-geometry-a-08.body:
Put $M=(0,0)$ and $A=(0,1)$. Then line $BA$ makes $80^\circ$ with the horizontal, $BM$ makes $60^\circ$, $CA$ makes $50^\circ$ with the horizontal on the other side and $CM$ makes $20^\circ$ (these come from the given angles). The heights of $B$ and $C$ above $M$ are $\frac{\tan20^\circ}{\tan20^\circ-\tan50^\circ}$ and $\frac{\tan60^\circ}{\tan60^\circ-\tan80^\circ}$. They are equal iff $\tan20^\circ\tan80^\circ=\tan60^\circ\tan50^\circ$, i.e. $\tan20^\circ\tan40^\circ\tan80^\circ=\tan60^\circ$, which is the identity $\tan x\tan(60^\circ-x)\tan(60^\circ+x)=\tan3x$ at $x=20^\circ$. So $BC\perp AM$, and $\angle MBC=90^\circ-\angle MAB-\angle MBA=90^\circ-10^\circ-20^\circ=60^\circ$.

**Answer: 60**
